claim: The genome-scale transcriptional programs that specify the mammalian trachea and esophagus are unknown.
source: The genome-scale transcriptional programs that specify the mammalian trachea and esophagus are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: NKX2-1 and SOX2 are hypothesized to be co-repressive master regulators of tracheoesophageal fates.
source: Though NKX2-1 and SOX2 are hypothesized to be co-repressive master regulators of tracheoesophageal fates, this is untested at a whole transcriptomic scale and their downstream networks remain unidentified.
evidence: The abstract states this as a hypothesis that has not been tested at the transcriptomic scale.

claim: The majority of the tracheal and esophageal transcriptome is NKX2-1 independent.
source: we delineate the NKX2-1 transcriptional program in tracheoesophageal specification, and discover that the majority of the tracheal and esophageal transcriptome is NKX2-1 independent.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data comparing Nkx2-1-/- mutants to wild type.

claim: NKX2-1 binds directly to Shh and Wnt7b.
source: Finally, we discover that NKX2-1 binds directly to Shh and Wnt7b and regulates their expression to control mesenchymal specification to cartilage and smooth muscle, coupling epithelial identity with mesenchymal specification.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing NKX2-1 binding at these loci.

claim: NKX2-1 regulates Shh and Wnt7b expression to control mesenchymal specification to cartilage and smooth muscle.
source: Finally, we discover that NKX2-1 binds directly to Shh and Wnt7b and regulates their expression to control mesenchymal specification to cartilage and smooth muscle, coupling epithelial identity with mesenchymal specification.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in mutants and observation of mesenchymal phenotypes.

claim: Formation of the trachea and esophagus requires signals from the splanchnic mesenchyme which specify ventral and dorsal domains of the foregut endoderm tube.
source: Formation of the trachea and esophagus requires signals from the splanchnic mesenchyme which specify ventral and dorsal domains of the foregut endoderm tube, resulting in lung bud outgrowth and the initiation of physical separation of the trachea and esophagus (Billmyre et al., 2015; Cardoso and Lü, 2006; Domyan et al., 2011; Goss et al., 2009; Harris-Johnson et al., 2009; Morrisey et al., 2013; Rankin et al., 2018; Rankin et al., 2016; Shannon et al., 1998; Stevens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The tracheal epithelium is composed of multi-ciliated, secretory, and basal cells within a pseudostratified columnar monolayer.
source: Ultimately, the tracheal epithelium is composed of multi-ciliated, secretory, and basal cells within a pseudostratified columnar monolayer which is surrounded by mesenchyme-derived ventral cartilaginous rings, and dorsal smooth muscle of the trachealis.
evidence: This describes the known cellular composition of the mature trachea.

claim: The tracheal epithelium is surrounded by mesenchyme-derived ventral cartilaginous rings and dorsal smooth muscle of the trachealis.
source: Ultimately, the tracheal epithelium is composed of multi-ciliated, secretory, and basal cells within a pseudostratified columnar monolayer which is surrounded by mesenchyme-derived ventral cartilaginous rings, and dorsal smooth muscle of the trachealis.
evidence: This describes the known mesenchymal structures surrounding the trachea.

claim: The esophagus consists of a stratified squamous keratinized epithelium surrounded by smooth muscle.
source: The esophagus consists ultimately of a stratified squamous keratinized epithelium surrounded by smooth muscle.
evidence: This describes the known structure of the mature esophagus.

claim: Early failure of tracheoesophageal fate specification can result in tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) or tracheal agenesis (TA).
source: Early failure of tracheoesophageal (TE) fate specification can result in an unseparated common foregut endoderm tube, producing common congenital pathologies known as tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) or tracheal agenesis (TA) (Billmyre et al., 2015; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010; Sher and Liu, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on congenital pathologies.

claim: NKX2-1 (TTF1) is the earliest marker of tracheal and lung fate.
source: The earliest marker of tracheal and lung fate is the transcription factor NKX2-1 (TTF1) which is expressed in the ventral foregut in a pattern complementary to the dorsally enriched expression of the transcription factor SOX2 (Guazzi et al., 1990; Minoo et al., 1999; Mizuno et al., 1991; Que et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: NKX2-1 is expressed in the ventral foregut in a pattern complementary to the dorsally enriched expression of SOX2.
source: The earliest marker of tracheal and lung fate is the transcription factor NKX2-1 (TTF1) which is expressed in the ventral foregut in a pattern complementary to the dorsally enriched expression of the transcription factor SOX2 (Guazzi et al., 1990; Minoo et al., 1999; Mizuno et al., 1991; Que et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of Nkx2-1 in mice resulted in upregulation of SOX2 in the ventral endoderm.
source: Disruption of Nkx2-1 in mice resulted in upregulation of SOX2 in the ventral endoderm and differentiation of the adjacent mesenchyme into smooth muscle rather than tracheal cartilage (Minoo et al., 1999; Que et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Disruption of Nkx2-1 in mice resulted in differentiation of the adjacent mesenchyme into smooth muscle rather than tracheal cartilage.
source: Disruption of Nkx2-1 in mice resulted in upregulation of SOX2 in the ventral endoderm and differentiation of the adjacent mesenchyme into smooth muscle rather than tracheal cartilage (Minoo et al., 1999; Que et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hypomorphic disruption of Sox2 in mice resulted in upregulation of dorsal NKX2-1.
source: Conversely, hypomorphic disruption of Sox2 in mice resulted in upregulation of dorsal NKX2-1 and a conversion of the stratified esophageal epithelium to a simple columnar epithelium surrounded by smooth muscle that histologically resembles that of the trachea (Que et al., 2007; Teramoto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hypomorphic disruption of Sox2 in mice resulted in conversion of the stratified esophageal epithelium to a simple columnar epithelium surrounded by smooth muscle that histologically resembles that of the trachea.
source: Conversely, hypomorphic disruption of Sox2 in mice resulted in upregulation of dorsal NKX2-1 and a conversion of the stratified esophageal epithelium to a simple columnar epithelium surrounded by smooth muscle that histologically resembles that of the trachea (Que et al., 2007; Teramoto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Knockdown of SOX2 in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived dorsal foregut cells resulted in upregulation of NKX2-1.
source: Similarly, knockdown of SOX2 in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived dorsal foregut cells resulted in upregulation of NKX2-1, and forced expression of SOX2 in hiPSC-derived ventral foregut cells repressed NKX2-1 (Trisno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Forced expression of SOX2 in hiPSC-derived ventral foregut cells repressed NKX2-1.
source: Similarly, knockdown of SOX2 in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived dorsal foregut cells resulted in upregulation of NKX2-1, and forced expression of SOX2 in hiPSC-derived ventral foregut cells repressed NKX2-1 (Trisno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: NKX2-1 and SOX2 form a co-repressive master regulatory switch to define tracheal and esophageal cell fates.
source: Together these data have given rise to a model in which NKX2-1 and SOX2 form a co-repressive master regulatory switch to define tracheal and esophageal cell fates (Billmyre et al., 2015; Domyan et al., 2011; Que et al., 2007; Teramoto et al., 2019; Trisno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a model based on previous work, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of WNT signaling from the endoderm to the tracheal mesenchyme results in a loss of tracheal cartilage and a corresponding expansion of smooth muscle.
source: For example, loss of WNT signaling from the endoderm to the tracheal mesenchyme results in a loss of tracheal cartilage and a corresponding expansion of smooth muscle (Hou et al., 2019; Kishimoto et al., 2019; Snowball et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SHH signaling regulates smooth muscle specification in multiple contexts.
source: SHH signaling regulates smooth muscle specification in multiple contexts (Huycke et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of SHH signaling from the airway and intestinal epithelium results in loss of smooth muscle formation.
source: and loss of SHH signaling from the airway and intestinal epithelium results in loss of smooth muscle formation (Kim et al., 2015; Litingtung et al., 1998; Pepicelli et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of SHH signaling results in mispatterning of tracheal cartilage.
source: and loss of SHH signaling from the airway and intestinal epithelium results in loss of smooth muscle formation (Kim et al., 2015; Litingtung et al., 1998; Pepicelli et al., 1998) and mispatterning of tracheal cartilage (Miller et al., 2004; Sala et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 6407 single-cell transcriptomes were generated at E10.5, comprising 5 cell clusters.
source: We generated 6407 single-cell transcriptomes at E10.5, comprising 5 cell clusters, and 10,493 single-cell transcriptomes at E11.5, comprising 7 cell clusters
evidence: This is a direct report of the scRNA-seq data generated.

claim: 10,493 single-cell transcriptomes were generated at E11.5, comprising 7 cell clusters.
source: We generated 6407 single-cell transcriptomes at E10.5, comprising 5 cell clusters, and 10,493 single-cell transcriptomes at E11.5, comprising 7 cell clusters
evidence: This is a direct report of the scRNA-seq data generated.

claim: Sox9 is a marker of developing lung epithelium.
source: Similarly, Sox9, a marker of developing lung epithelium (Herriges et al., 2012; Perl et al., 2005; Rockich et al., 2013), marked a subset of Nkx2-1-positive respiratory cells, enabling us to distinguish distal lung from trachea
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell clusters were defined as lung, trachea, esophagus, and pharynx using differential expression analysis and RNAscope fluorescent in-situ hybridization.
source: Using differential expression analysis for each cell cluster and RNAscope fluorescent in-situ hybridization, we defined cell clusters as lung, trachea, esophagus, and pharynx (Figure 1a–l'', Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–m, Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a)
evidence: This describes the methods used to identify cell clusters.

claim: A cluster corresponding to the ultimobranchial body was identified in the scRNA-seq data.
source: as well as a cluster corresponding to the ultimobranchial body, a derivative of the pharyngeal endoderm that gives rise to the follicular cells of the thyroid (Nilsson and Fagman, 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is supported by citation and figure reference.

claim: Within the E11.5 lung, a cluster with unique expression of known distal lung markers such as Bmp4 was identified.
source: Within the E11.5 lung, we identified a cluster with unique expression of known distal lung markers such as Bmp4 (Weaver et al., 1999; Figure 1—figure supplement 3c, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by citation and figure reference.

claim: The proximodistal lung axis can be identified by markers in the scRNA-seq dataset.
source: demonstrating that the proximodistal lung axis can be identified by markers in our dataset.
evidence: This is an inference from the identification of distal lung markers.

claim: Signatures of proliferation divided both the trachea and lung clusters at E11.5.
source: Signatures of proliferation also divided both the trachea and lung clusters at E11.5 (Figure 1b, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by figure reference and source data.

claim: Irx2, Tppp3, and Ly6h exhibit enrichment in the ventral foregut at E10.5.
source: Notably, we also discovered genes such as Tppp3, Pcdh10, Ly6h, and Cldn18 that exhibited enrichment in the ventral foregut at E10.5 (Figure 1c,g–i", Figure 1—figure supplement 2e-j')
evidence: This is supported by figure references showing expression patterns.

claim: Tppp3, Pcdh10, Ly6h, and Cldn18 specifically mark the trachea and proximal airway at E11.5.
source: and specifically marked the trachea and proximal airway at E11.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by figure reference showing expression patterns.

claim: The trachea and proximal airway are actively transcriptionally specified and at least somewhat distinct from the lung during early respiratory development.
source: Our discovery of this gene class indicates that the trachea and proximal airway are actively transcriptionally specified and at least somewhat distinct from the lung during early respiratory development.
evidence: This is an inference from the identification of trachea-specific markers.

claim: All tracheal and esophageal markers identified were dorsoventrally restricted in the common foregut of E10.5 embryos prior to physical separation of the trachea and esophagus.
source: All tracheal and esophageal markers we identified and validated were dorsoventrally restricted in the common foregut of E10.5 embryos prior to physical separation of the trachea and esophagus, consistent with extensive fate specification before TE separation (Billmyre et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the expression patterns observed in the data and citation.

claim: Differential expression analysis between Nkx2-1-/- and WT foregut epithelium identified 257 NKX2-1-dependent genes.
source: Differential expression analysis between Nkx2-1-/- and WT foregut epithelium identified 257 NKX2-1-dependent genes, with 109 genes upregulated and 148 genes downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: 109 genes were upregulated in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts compared to WT.
source: Differential expression analysis between Nkx2-1-/- and WT foregut epithelium identified 257 NKX2-1-dependent genes, with 109 genes upregulated and 148 genes downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: 148 genes were downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts compared to WT.
source: Differential expression analysis between Nkx2-1-/- and WT foregut epithelium identified 257 NKX2-1-dependent genes, with 109 genes upregulated and 148 genes downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Genes that were upregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants were enriched in cells of the esophagus and pharynx.
source: We found that genes that were upregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants were enriched in cells of the esophagus and pharynx (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the scRNA-seq data and figure references.

claim: Genes that were downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants were enriched in tracheal and lung cells.
source: and genes that were downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants were enriched in tracheal and lung cells (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the scRNA-seq data and figure references.

claim: NKX2-1 positively regulates tracheal genes and negatively regulates esophageal genes.
source: Together, these data define the NKX2-1 transcriptional program in early TE development and support the hypothesis that, within this program, NKX2-1 positively regulates tracheal genes and negatively regulates esophageal genes.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential expression analysis.

claim: All Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos examined exhibited a complete failure of foregut separation.
source: All Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos we examined exhibited a complete failure of foregut separation (n = 8/8 embryos).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mutant analysis.

claim: Irx2, Ly6h, and Nrp2 are tracheal-specific and maintained in the ventral epithelium of the unseparated foregut tube in E11.5 Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos.
source: Using RNAscope, we found Irx2, Ly6h, and Nrp2 to be tracheal-specific and maintained in the ventral epithelium of the unseparated foregut tube in E11.5 Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos (Figure 3a–f'; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope data and figure references.

claim: Dcn, Ackr3, and Meis2 are esophageal-specific and maintained in the dorsal region of the common foregut tube in Nkx2-1-TrKO foreguts.
source: Likewise, we found Dcn, Ackr3, and Meis2 to be esophageal-specific and maintained in the dorsal region of the common foregut tube in Nkx2-1-TrKO foreguts (Figure 3g–l'; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by RNAscope data and figure references.

claim: The esophageal genes LRIG1 and PITX1 were maintained in the dorsal region of Nkx2-1-/- foreguts.
source: Immunofluorescent staining also showed that the esophageal genes LRIG1 and PITX1 were maintained in the dorsal region of Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data and figure reference.

claim: Nkx2-1-/- mutant foreguts do not undergo a complete tracheal-to-esophageal fate conversion.
source: These data indicate the presence of an NKX2-1-independent transcriptional program within the developing trachea and esophagus, and suggest that Nkx2-1-/- mutant foreguts do not undergo a complete tracheal-to-esophageal fate conversion.
evidence: This is an inference from the maintenance of tracheal and esophageal markers in mutants.

claim: Differential expression analysis identified 1126 genes enriched in the trachea of WT embryos.
source: Differential expression analysis identified 1126 genes enriched in the trachea and 809 genes enriched in the esophagus of WT embryos (Figure 3n, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the differential expression analysis results.

claim: Differential expression analysis identified 809 genes enriched in the esophagus of WT embryos.
source: Differential expression analysis identified 1126 genes enriched in the trachea and 809 genes enriched in the esophagus of WT embryos (Figure 3n, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the differential expression analysis results.

claim: Only 11% of tracheal-enriched genes in WT foreguts were affected by loss of NKX2-1.
source: Notably, only 11% of tracheal-enriched genes and 6% of esophageal-enriched genes in WT foreguts were affected by loss of NKX2-1, and the majority of tracheal- or esophageal-enriched genes were unchanged in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 3n).
evidence: This is a direct report of the comparison between WT and mutant transcriptomes.

claim: Only 6% of esophageal-enriched genes in WT foreguts were affected by loss of NKX2-1.
source: Notably, only 11% of tracheal-enriched genes and 6% of esophageal-enriched genes in WT foreguts were affected by loss of NKX2-1, and the majority of tracheal- or esophageal-enriched genes were unchanged in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 3n).
evidence: This is a direct report of the comparison between WT and mutant transcriptomes.

claim: 15,861 genomic regions (peaks) shared between two biological replicates showed NKX2-1 binding.
source: We identified 15,861 genomic regions (peaks) shared between two biological replicates that showed NKX2-1 binding (Figure 4a, FDR < 0.00001)
evidence: This is a direct report of the ChIP-seq analysis results.

claim: NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks are centrally enriched for the known NKX2-1 motif.
source: and were centrally enriched for the known NKX2-1 motif (Figure 4b, p=3.4e-37).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of the ChIP-seq data.

claim: NKX2-1 binding was observed at the Nkx2-1 promoter and five binding sites within 10 kb of the Nkx2-1 gene.
source: We observed NKX2-1 binding at the Nkx2-1 promoter and five binding sites within 10 kb of the Nkx2-1 gene, consistent with previous data suggesting that NKX2-1 autoregulates its own expression (Nakazato et al., 1997; Oguchi and Kimura, 1998; Tagne et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and citations to previous work.

claim: NKX2-1 autoregulates its own expression.
source: We observed NKX2-1 binding at the Nkx2-1 promoter and five binding sites within 10 kb of the Nkx2-1 gene, consistent with previous data suggesting that NKX2-1 autoregulates its own expression (Nakazato et al., 1997; Oguchi and Kimura, 1998; Tagne et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and citations to previous work.

claim: NKX2-1 binding was observed at the Sox2 promoter and four binding sites within the Sox2 locus.
source: and also observed binding of NKX2-1 at the Sox2 promoter and four binding sites within the Sox2 locus, suggesting direct repression of Sox2 by NKX2-1 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: NKX2-1 directly represses Sox2.
source: and also observed binding of NKX2-1 at the Sox2 promoter and four binding sites within the Sox2 locus, suggesting direct repression of Sox2 by NKX2-1 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq data showing binding and the known repressive relationship.

claim: NKX2-1 binding was observed at the promoter of Pcdh10, Tppp3, and Klf5.
source: In addition, NKX2-1 binding was observed at the promoter of genes such as Pcdh10, Tppp3, and Klf5 that we identified as specific markers of the tracheal and esophageal lineages by scRNA-seq (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Pcdh10, Tppp3, and Klf5 may be direct targets of NKX2-1 regulation.
source: In addition, NKX2-1 binding was observed at the promoter of genes such as Pcdh10, Tppp3, and Klf5 that we identified as specific markers of the tracheal and esophageal lineages by scRNA-seq (Figure 4c), suggesting that these genes may also be direct targets of NKX2-1 regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq data showing binding.

claim: NKX2-1-dependent genes were associated with NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks at a higher frequency than observed at random.
source: Genome-wide comparison of NKX2-1-bound genes with the Nkx2-1-/- de-regulated transcriptome revealed that NKX2-1-dependent genes were associated with NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks at a higher frequency than observed at random (Figure 4d, Fisher's exact test, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes that are downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants are more frequently associated with NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks.
source: Furthermore, when we divided NKX2-1-dependent genes into those that were upregulated or downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants, we found that genes that are downregulated in Nkx2-1-/- mutants are more frequently associated with NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks (Figure 4d, Fisher's exact test, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: NKX2-1 is a direct positive regulator of tracheal-specific genes.
source: These data suggest that whereas NKX2-1 is a direct positive regulator of tracheal-specific genes, repression of esophageal-specific genes may more often be indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing more frequent binding at downregulated genes.

claim: Repression of esophageal-specific genes by NKX2-1 may more often be indirect.
source: These data suggest that whereas NKX2-1 is a direct positive regulator of tracheal-specific genes, repression of esophageal-specific genes may more often be indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing less frequent binding at upregulated genes.

claim: All Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO embryos examined exhibited a complete failure of foregut separation.
source: Similar to the Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos, all Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO embryos we examined exhibited a complete failure of foregut separation (n = 6/6 embryos).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: Expression of Pcdh10 and Tppp3 requires NKX2-1 but not upregulation of SOX2.
source: The expression of the tracheal-specific genes Pcdh10 and Tppp3 was decreased in Nkx2-1-TrKO and Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO ventral foreguts indicating that their expression requires NKX2-1 but not upregulation of SOX2 (Figure 5d–i')
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in compound mutants.

claim: Expression of Klf5 was upregulated in the ventral foreguts of Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos.
source: Conversely, expression of the esophageal-specific genes Klf5 and Has2 was upregulated in the ventral foreguts of Nkx2-1-TrKO, as predicted from our RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5j–o').
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in mutants.

claim: Expression of Has2 was upregulated in the ventral foreguts of Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos.
source: Conversely, expression of the esophageal-specific genes Klf5 and Has2 was upregulated in the ventral foreguts of Nkx2-1-TrKO, as predicted from our RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5j–o').
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in mutants.

claim: Klf5 expression was increased in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO mutants.
source: Interestingly, whereas Klf5 expression was also increased in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1tr/tr; Sox2tr/tr mutants (arrowhead Figure 5l,l'), Has2 expression was not, with the exception of a few cells that retain SOX2 expression ventrally (arrowhead in Figure 5o,o').
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in compound mutants.

claim: Has2 expression was not increased in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO mutants, with the exception of a few cells that retain SOX2 expression ventrally.
source: Interestingly, whereas Klf5 expression was also increased in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1tr/tr; Sox2tr/tr mutants (arrowhead Figure 5l,l'), Has2 expression was not, with the exception of a few cells that retain SOX2 expression ventrally (arrowhead in Figure 5o,o').
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in compound mutants.

claim: Upregulation of Has2 in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos depends on the upregulation of SOX2 in this region.
source: Thus, while Klf5 and Has2 were both repressed by NKX2-1, upregulation of Has2 in the ventral foregut of Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos appears to also depend on the upregulation of SOX2 in this region.
evidence: This is inferred from the compound mutant analysis showing Has2 requires SOX2 for upregulation.

claim: NKX2-1 regulation results from both direct activation of tracheal genes and repression of esophageal genes, as well as the indirect suppression of target genes through the repression of Sox2.
source: Together, these results revealed that NKX2-1 regulation results from both direct activation of tracheal genes and repression of esophageal genes, as well as the indirect suppression of target genes through the repression of Sox2, illustrating the complex relationship between these two transcription factors with opposing expression patterns.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: Nkx2-1-/- mutants exhibit a dramatic reduction and disorganization of tracheal cartilage with expansion of the smooth muscle.
source: We confirmed previous reports of a dramatic reduction and disorganization of tracheal cartilage with expansion of the smooth muscle in Nkx2-1-/- mutants, and additionally observed malformation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilage (n = 3/3 embryos, Figure 6a,o,p).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal preparations and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Nkx2-1-/- mutants exhibit malformation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilage.
source: We confirmed previous reports of a dramatic reduction and disorganization of tracheal cartilage with expansion of the smooth muscle in Nkx2-1-/- mutants, and additionally observed malformation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilage (n = 3/3 embryos, Figure 6a,o,p).
evidence: This is supported by skeletal preparations.

claim: Wnt7b expression decreased in Nkx2-1-/- foregut epithelium compared to WT.
source: Notably, Wnt7b expression decreased and Shh increased in Nkx2-1-/- foregut epithelium compared to WT (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Shh expression increased in Nkx2-1-/- foregut epithelium compared to WT.
source: Notably, Wnt7b expression decreased and Shh increased in Nkx2-1-/- foregut epithelium compared to WT (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Wnt7b is expressed in the tracheal epithelium in WT E11.5 and E13.5 embryos.
source: In WT E11.5 and E13.5 embryos, Wnt7b is expressed in the tracheal epithelium and Shh is expressed more strongly in the esophageal epithelium (Gerhardt et al., 2018; Litingtung et al., 1998; Rajagopal et al., 2008; Snowball et al., 2015; Figure 6c,f,i,m).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations.

claim: Shh is expressed more strongly in the esophageal epithelium in WT E11.5 and E13.5 embryos.
source: In WT E11.5 and E13.5 embryos, Wnt7b is expressed in the tracheal epithelium and Shh is expressed more strongly in the esophageal epithelium (Gerhardt et al., 2018; Litingtung et al., 1998; Rajagopal et al., 2008; Snowball et al., 2015; Figure 6c,f,i,m).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations.

claim: NKX2-1 binds at three sites 20 kb and 60 kb upstream and 20 kb downstream of the Wnt7b gene.
source: We examined our NKX2-1 ChIP-seq data to determine whether NKX2-1 binds directly to Wnt7b and Shh in the trachea and observed binding at three sites 20 kb and 60 kb upstream and 20 kb downstream of the Wnt7b gene.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: NKX2-1 binds at two sites within the Shh gene, and two additional peaks 50 kb and 150 kb upstream of Shh.
source: We also observed two NKX2-1 ChIP-seq peaks within the Shh gene, and two additional peaks 50 kb and 150 kb upstream of Shh, consistent with the possibility of direct regulation by NKX2-1 (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data.

claim: Wnt7b and Shh are targets of NKX2-1 regulation in the developing foregut.
source: Together, these data indicate that Wnt7b and Shh are targets of NKX2-1 regulation in the developing foregut.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq and expression data.

claim: Wnt7b expression was lost in both Nkx2-1-TrKO and Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts.
source: Wnt7b expression was lost in both Nkx2-1-TrKO and Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts, suggesting that NKX2-1 regulates Wnt7b independently of regulation by SOX2 (Figure 6c–e').
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in compound mutants.

claim: NKX2-1 regulates Wnt7b independently of regulation by SOX2.
source: Wnt7b expression was lost in both Nkx2-1-TrKO and Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts, suggesting that NKX2-1 regulates Wnt7b independently of regulation by SOX2 (Figure 6c–e').
evidence: This is inferred from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: The increase in Shh expression in the ventral foregut observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos was not observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts.
source: However, the increase in Shh expression in the ventral foregut observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos was not observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts (Figure 6f–h')
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis in compound mutants.

claim: SOX2 is required for upregulation of Shh in the ventral foregut.
source: However, the increase in Shh expression in the ventral foregut observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO embryos was not observed in Nkx2-1-TrKO; Sox2-TrKO foreguts (Figure 6f–h'), indicating that SOX2 is required for upregulation of Shh in the ventral foregut.
evidence: This is inferred from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: Wnt7b expression is positively regulated by NKX2-1 but not subject to regulation by SOX2.
source: Thus, Wnt7b expression is positively regulated by NKX2-1 but not subject to regulation by SOX2, whereas the dorsally restricted expression of Shh is mediated by the combined action of NKX2-1 and SOX2.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: The dorsally restricted expression of Shh is mediated by the combined action of NKX2-1 and SOX2.
source: Thus, Wnt7b expression is positively regulated by NKX2-1 but not subject to regulation by SOX2, whereas the dorsally restricted expression of Shh is mediated by the combined action of NKX2-1 and SOX2.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the compound mutant analysis.

claim: In WT embryos, Axin2 expression was localized to the ventral tracheal mesenchyme where SOX9+ cartilage progenitor cells are found.
source: Whereas in WT embryos Axin2 expression was localized to the ventral tracheal mesenchyme where SOX9+ cartilage progenitor cells are found, in Nkx2-1-/- mutants Axin2 expression was decreased and correlated with disorganized SOX9 expression (Figure 6i–l, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data.

claim: In Nkx2-1-/- mutants, Axin2 expression was decreased and correlated with disorganized SOX9 expression.
source: Whereas in WT embryos Axin2 expression was localized to the ventral tracheal mesenchyme where SOX9+ cartilage progenitor cells are found, in Nkx2-1-/- mutants Axin2 expression was decreased and correlated with disorganized SOX9 expression (Figure 6i–l, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The decrease in Axin2 expression was more dramatic in the caudal foregut, consistent with the increased severity of cartilage specification defects in this region.
source: This decrease in Axin2 expression was more dramatic in the caudal foregut, consistent with the increased severity of cartilage specification defects in this region seen in skeletal preparations (Figure 6a) and as visualized by SOX9 localization in Nkx2-1-/- foreguts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c–e).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and skeletal preparation data.

claim: In E11.5 and E13.5 Nkx2-1-/- foreguts, increased expression of Shh in the ventral foregut epithelium compared to WT was mirrored by an increase in Ptch1 expression in the surrounding mesenchyme.
source: In E11.5 and E13.5 Nkx2-1-/- foreguts, increased expression of Shh in the ventral foregut epithelium compared to WT was mirrored by an increase in Ptch1 expression in the surrounding mesenchyme (Figure 6m,n; Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: The increase in Ptch1 expression corresponded with the increase in smooth muscle as visualized by ACTA2 (i.e. α-SMA) surrounding Nkx2-1-/- foreguts compared to WT.
source: This increase in Ptch1 expression also corresponded with the increase in smooth muscle as visualized by ACTA2 (i.e. α-SMA) surrounding Nkx2-1-/- foreguts compared to WT (Figure 6m–p, S8c,f,g).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data.

claim: NKX2-1 and SOX2 regulate epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk via WNT and SHH signaling to instruct mesenchymal differentiation.
source: Thus, our data show that in addition to regulating a subset of genes that define tracheoesophageal epithelial identity at this stage, NKX2-1 and SOX2 regulate epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk via WNT and SHH signaling to instruct mesenchymal differentiation, explaining this aspect of the observed TE fate transformation in Nkx2-1-/- mutant foreguts (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the signaling and mesenchymal phenotype data.

claim: NKX2-1 loss does not cause a transcriptome-wide tracheal-to-esophageal conversion.
source: By performing scRNA-seq profiling on the endoderm at the onset of tracheal and esophageal development, and comparing this profile to Nkx2-1-/- mutant embryos, we find that NKX2-1 loss does not cause a transcriptome-wide tracheal-to-esophageal conversion, but rather results in changes in expression of a key subset of dorsoventrally restricted genes that can explain apparent fate-conversion phenotypes in the mesenchyme (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: Loss of NKX2-1 leads to adoption of a gastric transcriptional phenotype in adenocarcinoma and in the adult distal lung.
source: It has been previously demonstrated in adenocarcinoma and in the adult distal lung, that loss of NKX2-1 leads to adoption of a gastric transcriptional phenotype (Little et al., 2019; Snyder et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mesenchymal cues that induce lung and trachea development converge to establish ventral NKX2-1 expression.
source: Further, mesenchymal cues that induce lung and trachea development converge to establish ventral NKX2-1 expression, and Nkx2-1-/- mutant embryos exhibit dramatic epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by previous work and observations in this study.

claim: ISL1 transcription factor exhibits ventrally-restricted expression in the trachea and is required for normal NKX2-1 expression.
source: Interestingly, the ISL1 transcription factor has been recently identified to exhibit ventrally-restricted expression in the trachea and is required for normal NKX2-1 expression (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Isl1 is independent of NKX2-1.
source: Further, our data reveal that Isl1 is independent of NKX2-1 (Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that it resides hierarchically upstream of NKX2-1.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing no change in Isl1 expression in Nkx2-1 mutants.

claim: ISL1 resides hierarchically upstream of NKX2-1.
source: Further, our data reveal that Isl1 is independent of NKX2-1 (Figure 2—source data 1), indicating that it resides hierarchically upstream of NKX2-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the independence of Isl1 from NKX2-1 and its requirement for NKX2-1 expression.

claim: Direct binding of NKX2–1 occurs more often at genes that are normally expressed in the trachea.
source: We find, however, that direct binding of NKX2–1 occurs more often at genes that are normally expressed in the trachea, and loss of tracheal gene expression in Nkx2-1-/- mutants is not indirectly mediated by upregulation of SOX2.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and compound mutant analysis.

claim: Loss of tracheal gene expression in Nkx2-1-/- mutants is not indirectly mediated by upregulation of SOX2.
source: We find, however, that direct binding of NKX2–1 occurs more often at genes that are normally expressed in the trachea, and loss of tracheal gene expression in Nkx2-1-/- mutants is not indirectly mediated by upregulation of SOX2.
evidence: This is supported by compound mutant analysis.

claim: NKX2-1 more often positively regulates the tracheal gene expression program directly.
source: Together, these findings broadly support a model in which NKX2-1 more often positively regulates the tracheal gene expression program directly.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the ChIP-seq and mutant analysis.

claim: Normal tracheal cartilage specification requires WNT signaling from the tracheal epithelium to the mesenchyme.
source: Normal tracheal cartilage specification requires WNT signaling from the tracheal epithelium to the mesenchyme (Hou et al., 2019; Kishimoto et al., 2019; Snowball et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NKX2-1 positively regulates Wnt7b resulting in activation of a canonical WNT-signaling response in the adjacent ventral tracheal mesenchyme.
source: We find that NKX2-1 positively regulates Wnt7b resulting in activation of a canonical WNT-signaling response in the adjacent ventral tracheal mesenchyme.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis and Axin2 expression in the mesenchyme.

claim: An NKX2-1 independent mechanism also contributes to tracheal cartilage specification, as some disorganized cartilage still forms in Nkx2-1-/- mutants.
source: Our results differ from this finding but do support the possibility that an NKX2-1 independent mechanism also contributes to tracheal cartilage specification, as some disorganized cartilage still forms in Nkx2-1-/- mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of residual cartilage in mutants.

claim: NKX2-1 loss resulted in upregulation of Shh and increased SHH signal reception in the ventral mesenchyme.
source: In addition to regulating WNT signaling, we found that NKX2-1 loss resulted in upregulation of Shh and increased SHH signal reception in the ventral mesenchyme.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis of Shh and Ptch1.

claim: Upregulation of Shh in Nkx2-1 mutants likely contributes to disruption of tracheal cartilage and expansion of smooth muscle formation.
source: As HH signaling is a key regulator of smooth muscle formation in multiple contexts, and its disruption also results in perturbation of tracheal cartilage formation (Huycke et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2004; Sala et al., 2011), it is likely that this upregulation also contributes to disruption of tracheal cartilage and expansion of smooth muscle formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of HH signaling and the observed phenotypes.

claim: Key players in respiratory and gut specification are conserved between mice and humans.
source: While few genetic causes of foregut anomalies in humans have been identified, human stem cell models have indicated that key players in respiratory and gut specification are conserved between mice and humans (Ostrin et al., 2018; Trisno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
